title: Homework
text:
These optional exercises bring together the two topics from Session 2: writing functions and working with data frames. You’ll write a few small functions that take a data frame and the name of a column, and return something useful about that column. We’ll use the starwars dataset and the HES admissions data from Practical 2.
library(tidyverse)
Some exercises use the hospital admissions data from Practical 2 (hes_admissions.csv).
admissions <- read_csv("hes_admissions.csv")

title: Homework
section: Using a column name inside a function
text:
Using a column name inside a function
In Session 1 we saw that you can pull out a column from a data frame using $ or [[. Inside a function, [[ is the one to use, because it accepts the column name as a character string stored in an object:

col <- "height"
starwars[[col]]

 [1] 172 167  96 202 150 178 165  97 183 182 188 180 228 180 173 175 170 180  66
[20] 170 183 200 190 177 175 180 150  NA  88 160 193 191 170 185 196 224 206 183
[39] 137 112 183 163 175 180 178  79  94 122 163 188 198 196 171 184 188 264 188
[58] 196 185 157 183 183 170 166 165 193 191 183 168 198 229 213 167  96 193 191
[77] 178 216 234 188 178 206  NA  NA  NA  NA  NA


starwars$col would not work here: it looks for a column literally called col.

title: Homework
text:
Exercises

Write a function, column_mean(), that returns the mean of a column, ignoring missing values. It takes two arguments:

data: a data frame
col: the name of a column

Test it on the height column of starwars and the los_days column of admissions.







NoteSolution






column_mean <- function(data, col) {
  mean(data[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
}

column_mean(starwars, "height")

[1] 174.6049

column_mean(admissions, "los_days")

[1] 11.95874











NoteGoing further…





What happens if you give column_mean() a column that doesn’t exist (e.g. "weight"), or a character column (e.g. "name")? Update your function to check that the column exists and is numeric, and to stop with an informative error message if not. (Hint: names(data) gives the column names, and is.numeric() checks whether a vector is numeric.)
Without any checks, both calls return NA with a warning, which is easy to miss. Here is one solution:


Show the solution
column_mean <- function(data, col) {
  if (!(col %in% names(data))) {
    stop("Column '", col, "' not found in the data.")
  } else if (!is.numeric(data[[col]])) {
    stop("Column '", col, "' must be numeric.")
  }
  mean(data[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
}






Write a function, count_missing(), that returns the number of missing values in a column. How many are there in:

mass in starwars?
discharge_destination in admissions?








NoteSolution





is.na() returns TRUE for each missing value, and sum() counts the TRUE values.

count_missing <- function(data, col) {
  sum(is.na(data[[col]]))
}

count_missing(starwars, "mass")

[1] 28

count_missing(admissions, "discharge_destination")

[1] 67


There are 28 missing values in mass, and 67 in discharge_destination. (Remember from Practical 2 that a further 134 destinations are recorded as “UNK” or “Unknown”, which R doesn’t treat as missing.)




Write a function, column_summary(), that returns a one-row data frame for a numeric column, containing:

the mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, rounded to one decimal place
the number of missing values (use your count_missing() function from question 2)








NoteSolution






column_summary <- function(data, col) {
  x <- data[[col]]
  data.frame(
    column = col,
    mean = round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    sd = round(sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    min = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_missing = count_missing(data, col)
  )
}

column_summary(starwars, "height")

  column  mean   sd min max n_missing
1 height 174.6 34.8  66 264         6

column_summary(admissions, "los_days")

    column mean sd min  max n_missing
1 los_days   12  3   2 22.4         0






Write a function, keep_above(), that takes a data frame, a column name and a threshold, and keeps only the rows where that column is greater than the threshold. Use it to find:

characters in starwars with a mass over 100
spells in admissions longer than 14 days








TipHint





Inside filter(), you can refer to a column whose name is stored in an object using .data[[col]]. Alternatively, use [[ to make a logical vector and pass that to filter().









NoteSolution






keep_above <- function(data, col, threshold) {
  data |>
    filter(.data[[col]] > threshold)
}

keep_above(starwars, "mass", 100)

# A tibble: 10 × 14
   name     height  mass hair_color skin_color eye_color birth_year sex   gender
   <chr>     <int> <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <chr>          <dbl> <chr> <chr> 
 1 Darth V…    202   136 none       white      yellow          41.9 male  mascu…
 2 Owen La…    178   120 brown, gr… light      blue            52   male  mascu…
 3 Chewbac…    228   112 brown      unknown    blue           200   male  mascu…
 4 Jabba D…    175  1358 <NA>       green-tan… orange         600   herm… mascu…
 5 Jek Ton…    180   110 brown      fair       blue            NA   <NA>  <NA>  
 6 IG-88       200   140 none       metal      red             15   none  mascu…
 7 Bossk       190   113 none       green      red             53   male  mascu…
 8 Dexter …    198   102 none       brown      yellow          NA   male  mascu…
 9 Grievous    216   159 none       brown, wh… green, y…       NA   male  mascu…
10 Tarfful     234   136 brown      brown      blue            NA   male  mascu…
# ℹ 5 more variables: homeworld <chr>, species <chr>, films <list>,
#   vehicles <list>, starships <list>

keep_above(admissions, "los_days", 14) |>
  nrow()

[1] 1574


There are 10 characters with a mass over 100, and 1,574 spells longer than 14 days (the same as question 4 of Practical 2). Note that filter() drops rows where the condition is NA, so characters with a missing mass are not kept.
Here .data stands for “the data frame being filtered”, and .data[[col]] works just like data[[col]]. There are other ways of passing column names into dplyr functions: see Programming with dplyr if you’re interested.

title: Practical 1: Functions
text:
A function takes an input, does something with it, and returns a result

  
  INPUT
  FUNCTION
  OUTPUT

  
  
  
  
  

  
  
    
    radius = 5
  

  
  
    
    78.54
  

  
  
  
  
  circle_area(radius)

  
  pi * radius^2
  pi * 5^2
  = 78.54
In this practical you’ll write your own functions, starting with simple calculations and building up to functions that check their inputs and make decisions using if and else.

title: Practical 1: Functions
Practical 1: Functions
Practical 1: Functions
Homework
text: This section provides optional exercises for those who want to practise and solidify the concepts introduced in the practicals. The exercises focus on subsetting data frames using the penguins dataset, more advanced vector subsetting with conditionals, and control flow with if, else and ifelse().

title: Homework
text:
Creating new columns
With the penguins data frame:

Tabulate the number of missing values (NA) in the sex column.







TipHint





You’ll need to use the is.na and table functions.









NoteSolution






table(is.na(penguins[["sex"]]))


FALSE  TRUE 
  333    11 

# Or, equivalently:
table(is.na(penguins$sex))


FALSE  TRUE 
  333    11 

# This would also work, but is fairly verbose:
sum(is.na(penguins$sex))

[1] 11

sum(!is.na(penguins$sex))

[1] 333






Using assignment, create a new column, containing bill_len stored as an integer.







NoteSolution






penguins$bill_int <-  as.integer(penguins$bill_len)





Create a new column containing bill_dep formatted to two decimal places.







TipHint





You’ll need to use sprintf for this, with the format string "%.2f". See the help file for details.









NoteSolution






penguins$bill_depth_2dp <- sprintf("%.2f", penguins$bill_dep)





Use paste to concatenate the species and island columns. Store the result as a new column.







NoteSolution






penguins$species_island <-  paste(penguins$species, penguins$island)

title: Homework
text:
Months of the year

Define a character vector containing the months of the year (i.e., January, February, …, December).







NoteSolution






moy <- c(
  "January",
  "February",
  "March",
  "April",
  "May",
  "June",
  "July",
  "August",
  "September",
  "October",
  "November",
  "December"
)

# Or use the built-in constant 'month.name'
moy <- month.name

# NOTE: I'm using 'moy' as short for 'Months of the year', but you can use any
# label you like.





Select the third element of this vector.







NoteSolution






moy[3]

[1] "March"






Select the 6th, 7th, and 8th elements of this vector.







NoteSolution






moy[c(6, 7, 8)]

[1] "June"   "July"   "August"

# Or, even shorter:
moy[6:8]

[1] "June"   "July"   "August"






Select the last five elements of this vector.







NoteSolution






moy[8:12]

[1] "August"    "September" "October"   "November"  "December" 

# The above answer will work, but it assumes that
# there are always 12 elements in the vector. This
# is true for this example, but it's good practice
# to write code that can handle various input lengths.

tail(moy, 5)

[1] "August"    "September" "October"   "November"  "December" 






Select all months ending in “er” (Hint: str_ends).







TipUse the str_ends function





str_ends is a function that returns a logical value (TRUE or FALSE) indicating whether a string ends with a specified pattern.
To use the function, you’ll first need to load the tidyverse library:

library(tidyverse)










NoteSolution






moy[str_ends(moy, "er")]

[1] "September" "October"   "November"  "December" 






Select all months starting with “A” (Hint: str_starts).







NoteSolution






moy[str_starts(moy, "A")]

[1] "April"  "August"

# As always, there are multiple ways of achieving this.
# The above method is quite efficient, but you could
# also try:

# Using regular expressions:
moy[str_detect(moy, "^A")]

[1] "April"  "August"

# Using purrr
keep(moy, \(x) str_detect(x, "^A"))

[1] "April"  "August"

# Or, if you really want to over-complicate it:
a_months <- c()
for (m in moy) {
  if (substring(m, 1, 1) == "A") {
    a_months <- c(a_months, m)
  }
}  # You shouldn't do this! But try to see what's happening here.

title: Homework
text:
Control flow

Create an object x containing a single number. Then write an if/else statement that prints:

"positive" if x is greater than zero
"zero or negative" otherwise

Try it with a few different values of x.







NoteSolution






x <- -3
if (x > 0) {
  print("positive")
} else {
  print("zero or negative")
}

[1] "zero or negative"






Extend your answer to question 1 so that it prints "positive", "negative" or "zero".







TipHint





Use else if to add a second condition.









NoteSolution






x <- 0
if (x > 0) {
  print("positive")
} else if (x < 0) {
  print("negative")
} else {
  print("zero")
}

[1] "zero"






Select the body mass (body_mass) of the first penguin in the penguins dataset. Then use if/else to create an object called size that is:

"heavy" if the penguin weighs 4,000 grams or more
"light" otherwise








NoteSolution






first_mass <- penguins$body_mass[1]
if (first_mass >= 4000) {
  size <- "heavy"
} else {
  size <- "light"
}
size

[1] "light"






Now try to do the same for every penguin, by replacing penguins$body_mass[1] with penguins$body_mass. What happens, and why?







NoteSolution






if (penguins$body_mass >= 4000) {
  size <- "heavy"
} else {
  size <- "light"
}

Error in `if (penguins$body_mass >= 4000) ...`:
! the condition has length > 1


if expects a condition that is a single TRUE or FALSE. Here, the condition penguins$body_mass >= 4000 is a vector with one value per penguin, so R stops with an error.




Use ifelse() to create a new column in penguins called size, containing "heavy" or "light" for every penguin. Tabulate the new column with table().







NoteSolution






penguins$size <- ifelse(penguins$body_mass >= 4000, "heavy", "light")
table(penguins$size)


heavy light 
  177   165 






Two penguins have a missing body mass. What value do they get in your new size column? Check using table(penguins$size, useNA = "ifany").







NoteSolution






table(penguins$size, useNA = "ifany")


heavy light  <NA> 
  177   165     2 


They are NA. When the condition is NA, ifelse() can’t decide between "heavy" and "light", so it returns NA. This is usually what you want: it keeps missing values missing.




Use ifelse() with the moy vector you created above to label each month as "summer" (June, July and August) or "not summer".







TipHint





The %in% operator checks whether each element of one vector appears in another, e.g. moy %in% c("June", "July").









NoteSolution






ifelse(moy %in% c("June", "July", "August"), "summer", "not summer")

 [1] "not summer" "not summer" "not summer" "not summer" "not summer"
 [6] "summer"     "summer"     "summer"     "not summer" "not summer"
[11] "not summer" "not summer"






Write a for loop that prints a sentence for each month in moy, e.g. "Month 1 is January". Then find a way to get the same sentences without a loop.







TipHint





seq_along(moy) gives the sequence 1, 2, ..., 12, one number per element of moy. Use paste() to join text and numbers together.









NoteSolution






for (i in seq_along(moy)) {
  print(paste("Month", i, "is", moy[i]))
}

[1] "Month 1 is January"
[1] "Month 2 is February"
[1] "Month 3 is March"
[1] "Month 4 is April"
[1] "Month 5 is May"
[1] "Month 6 is June"
[1] "Month 7 is July"
[1] "Month 8 is August"
[1] "Month 9 is September"
[1] "Month 10 is October"
[1] "Month 11 is November"
[1] "Month 12 is December"


paste() is vectorised, so it can do all twelve months at once:

paste("Month", seq_along(moy), "is", moy)

 [1] "Month 1 is January"   "Month 2 is February"  "Month 3 is March"    
 [4] "Month 4 is April"     "Month 5 is May"       "Month 6 is June"     
 [7] "Month 7 is July"      "Month 8 is August"    "Month 9 is September"
[10] "Month 10 is October"  "Month 11 is November" "Month 12 is December"


This is why we rarely need loops in R: most functions already work on every element of a vector.

This practical introduces the basics of using RStudio Desktop1, including navigating its interface and using keyboard shortcuts.

title: RStudio basics
text:
Opening RStudio

Open RStudio on your computer2.
Open a new script editor within RStudio.
Practise using keyboard shortcuts:

Switch between the console and script editor with Ctrl + 1 and Ctrl + 2.
Scroll through the console history with ↑ and ↓.
Search the console history with Ctrl + r.
Clear the console screen with Ctrl + l.

(Optional) Pick a colour scheme in the settings.
Review the RStudio cheatsheet. What is the keyboard shortcut to comment (and uncomment) the selected text?

title: RStudio basics
text:
Using R as a calculator
Type at the console to answer the following questions.

What is \(5^7\)?







NoteSolution






5^7

[1] 78125

# Or, another way of writing this:
5**7

[1] 78125






What is the area of a circle with radius 5cm?







NoteSolution






# We could have approximated pi, for example:

3.14 * 5^2

[1] 78.5

# However, R has a built-in constant 'pi' object (see ?pi) that we can use
# instead:

pi * 5^2

[1] 78.53982






And the circumference?







NoteSolution






2 * pi * 5

[1] 31.41593

title: RStudio basics
text:
Getting help

Check the help for the fivenum function.
What does the na.rm argument do?
How can you calculate the modulo of two numbers?







TipHint





The modulo is the remainder after division of one number by another; see here for details. You may need to search online to answer this question.









NoteSolution





na.rm = TRUE removes missing values (NA) before the calculation. The modulo operator is %%:

fivenum(c(1, 5, 2, NA, 8), na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 1.0 1.5 3.5 6.5 8.0

17 %% 5

[1] 2

title: RStudio basics
text:
Creating objects

Define two new objects containing your first and last name as strings.







NoteSolution






# Example for my name:

first_name <- "Ewan"
last_name <- "Carr"





Use the paste command to concatenate these objects.







NoteSolution






paste(first_name, last_name)

[1] "Ewan Carr"

# Note that we haven't stored the result. R will print the output to the
# console, but then forget the result. We need to assign the output to a
# new object to store it in memory:

full_name <- paste(first_name, last_name)





Repeat the calculation of the circumference of a circle. This time:

Define a new variable radius that contains the value 5.
Use this variable in your calculation.








NoteSolution






radius <- 5

2 * pi * radius

[1] 31.41593











TipReflection




What happens if you don’t assign something?
How can you tell what objects are currently assigned?




Practise using str and typeof to check the structure and types of the objects you just created.







NoteSolution






str(first_name)

 chr "Ewan"

typeof(first_name)

[1] "character"

str(radius)

 num 5

typeof(radius)

[1] "double"






Remove an object from memory using rm or via the RStudio “Environment” pane.







NoteSolution






rm(first_name)
rm(last_name)
rm(radius)

title: RStudio basics
text:
Working with vectors

Create three vectors:

A sequence of numbers from 1 to 5;

The letters a, b, c, d, e;

Five random numbers.








TipHint





Use the functions c, seq, rnorm(5).









NoteSolution






# A sequence of numbers
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
x <- seq(1, 5, 1)
x <- 1:5

# Letters a, b, c, d, e
y <- c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e")
y <- letters[1:5]

# Five random numbers
z <- rnorm(5)





Create two vectors, a and b, each containing 10 random numbers (using rnorm).







NoteSolution






a <- rnorm(10)
b <- rnorm(10)





Add each value of a to the corresponding value of b, creating a new vector of length 10.







NoteSolution






a + b

 [7] -0.53519302 -1.81596806 -0.67185024 -0.01485875

Add 5 to each value of a.







NoteSolution






a + 5

Combine the two vectors into a single vector of length 20.







NoteSolution






c(a, b)

[13]  2.29094258 -0.43269888 -0.32823210  2.51731262  0.38459802 -0.93647759

Footnotes


Referred to as ‘RStudio’ from here on.↩︎
If you’re having problems installing R, you can use Posit Cloud, an online version of RStudio.↩︎

title: Software
text:
You will need access to R and RStudio Desktop to participate in the practicals. R is the programming language, whereas RStudio Desktop is an editor we’ll use during the course.
You have two options:

Create a free account at https://posit.cloud, an online version of RStudio.
Install R and RStudio locally on your computer. See the links on this page. Note that you need to install both R and RStudio.

Once you’ve installed R and RStudio, install the tidyverse package by typing:

install.packages("tidyverse")

Please note:

You should use a recent version of R (e.g., 4.5.0 or higher). You can check which version you have installed by running sessionInfo() at the command prompt.
The online option is sufficient for this course. However, if you’d like to practise outside the course or run your own analyses, we recommend installing R locally.







Important



Please make sure you have access to a working R environment before the course starts. This could be the online option above or a local installation.

title: Welcome 👋
text:
This five-day course offers a comprehensive journey in R, from beginner to advanced levels, with a focus on practical data analysis, visualisation, and real-world applications in health data science.
Whatever your background or experience with R — whether you’re a total beginner or have some prior experience — we hope you find this course useful, enjoyable, and the beginning of a rewarding journey using R.








  Session 1Mon 2 NovBeginner
  Session 2Mon 9 NovIntermediate 1
  Session 3Mon 16 NovIntermediate 2
  Session 4Mon 23 NovAdvanced
  Session 5Mon 30 NovAdvanced


  Five Mondays, November 2026
  13:30–17:00 UK time
  Live on Zoom
  Slides and practicals appear here on the day

Each session mixes live lectures and practical exercises, with time for questions throughout.




Zoom link and site details. HDR UK will email you the Zoom link and details of this site before the course starts. Please keep that email to hand for each session.
Set up R and RStudio beforehand. Please make sure you have a working R environment before the first session. See the Software page for instructions.
Questions? For anything about joining or registration, contact HDR UK at learn@hdruk.ac.uk.




The course starts with the basics of R, including data types, subsetting, and control flow. We then move on to data manipulation, writing functions, and creating visualisations with ggplot2. Later sessions cover more advanced techniques such as iteration with purrr and working across many columns with across(). Practical exercises and a mini project provide hands-on experience with health-related datasets, along with dynamic reporting using Quarto.




Monday 2 November · Beginner

Welcome; what to expect when learning R
Objects and assignment; vectors; data types; missing values
Data frames; importing and exporting data; subsetting
Control flow: running code conditionally with if, else and ifelse(); a first look at for loops





Monday 9 November · Intermediate 1

Using and writing functions in R
Data manipulation with the tidyverse

Pipes; importing data
Selecting, filtering and sorting (select, filter, arrange)
Creating and modifying columns (mutate)
Recoding variables (if_else, case_when)









Monday 16 November · Intermediate 2

Keeping an analysis project organised
Merging and appending datasets (left_join, bind_rows)
Reshaping data between ‘wide’ and ‘long’ formats (pivot_longer, pivot_wider)
Grouping and summarising (group_by, summarise)





Monday 23 November · Advanced

Creating plots with ggplot2; factors
Dynamic reporting with Quarto; reproducible pipelines
Working with dates and times
Mini project: introduction






Monday 30 November · Advanced

Mini project: walkthrough and questions
Working efficiently with lists; introduction to purrr
Applying the same operation to many columns with across()
Text manipulation with regular expressions
Is my code slow? Timing and benchmarking
My favourite packages and things you should know

This outline is indicative. In practice we adjust the pace to suit the group, so topics may shift slightly between sessions.

title: About Me
text:
Ewan Carr
Reader in Biostatistics Department of Biostatistics & Health Informatics King’s College London



 King’s College London  GitHub  Bluesky
I’m a Reader in Biostatistics at King’s College London, where my research sits at the intersection of data science, digital health, and mental health care. I work on developing and evaluating clinical prediction models using real-world data—including electronic health records, smartphone-based assessments, and wearable sensors—with the goal of improving clinical decision-making and patient outcomes.
My current projects include tools to support stratified treatment for depression, methods for assessing fairness in predictive models, and software to guide sample size calculations in machine learning studies. Much of this work is done in collaboration with clinicians, computer scientists, and industry partners.
I’m committed to open, reproducible science and to building tools and workflows that make robust statistical methods more accessible to health researchers. I also teach and supervise across postgraduate programmes in statistics and health data science, and enjoy mentoring early-career researchers.

title: 🐣 Session 1: Beginner
text:
This first session provides a gentle introduction to R for those new to the language. We’ll explore what makes R a widely-used tool for data analysis and how it compares to alternatives such as Python, Stata, and SPSS.
We’ll cover essential building blocks of the R language, including using the console, installing packages, writing scripts, and navigating help files. You will learn about how to handle different data types, such as missing values and factors, and techniques for subsetting objects. We’ll finish by looking at control flow: running code conditionally with if, else and ifelse(), and a brief look at for loops.

title: Data frames
text:
Data frames

Combine the three vectors we created in Practical 1 into a new data frame. Remember to store the result as a new object.


x <- 1:5
y <- c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e")
z <- rnorm(5)







NoteSolution






my_data <- data.frame(x, y, z)





Count the number of rows and columns (e.g., nrow, ncol) and get the column names (names) of this data frame.







NoteSolution






# Assuming your data frame above was stored in an object called 'my_data':
nrow(my_data)

[1] 5

ncol(my_data)

[1] 3

names(my_data)

[1] "x" "y" "z"

title: Data frames
text:
Importing data
The starwars dataset is a built-in dataset provided by the dplyr package. It contains data on characters from the Star Wars universe, including variables such as name, height, mass, species, homeworld, and films.
To practise importing data, let’s first export the first 10 columns from the starwars dataset in a variety of formats:

1library(tidyverse)
2library(haven)
3library(writexl)

starwars <- starwars[, 1:10]

write_csv(starwars, file = "starwars.csv")
write_xlsx(starwars, path = "starwars.xlsx")
write_dta(starwars, path = "starwars.dta")
write_sav(starwars, path = "starwars.sav")


1

We’ll introduce the tidyverse package next session.

2

A package for importing and exporting data in different formats (e.g., Stata, SPSS).

3

A package for importing and exporting Microsoft Excel files.








Import starwars.csv using read_csv from the readr package.







NoteSolution






starwars_csv <- read_csv("starwars.csv")










NoteQuestions






What does this output mean?
What does the col_types argument do?





Import starwars.xlsx using read_xlsx from the readxl package.







NoteSolution






library(readxl)
starwars_xlsx  <- read_xlsx("starwars.xlsx")










TipUsing a function without loading its package





If you want to use a function without loading the package, you can type :: to refer to a specific function. For example:

readxl::read_xlsx("starwars.xlsx")

You might want to do this when you only need a single function once (e.g., importing).




Import starwars.dta (a Stata dataset) and starwars.sav (an SPSS dataset) using appropriate functions from the haven package.







NoteSolution






library(haven)

starwars_dta  <- read_dta("starwars.dta")
starwars_sav  <- read_sav("starwars.sav")

title: Data frames
text:
Subsetting
Subsetting is the process of selecting specific elements, rows, or columns from a data object based on conditions or indices.

Define a vector containing letters A to F.







NoteSolution






a_to_f <- c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F")







Note





You could also create this vector using the built-in LETTERS vector and subsetting:

a_to_f <- LETTERS[1:6]








Use subsetting to select:


The first element (i.e., A)
The third element (i.e., C)
All except the last element (i.e., A, B, C, D, E)







NoteSolution





We can select elements by position:

# First element
a_to_f[1]

[1] "A"

# Third element
a_to_f[3]

[1] "C"


To select ‘all except the last’ element, we need to use negation:

a_to_f[-6]

[1] "A" "B" "C" "D" "E"


Note that this only works if the vector has exactly six elements. We could instead define the position using length (i.e., the number of elements in the vector):

a_to_f[-length(a_to_f)]

[1] "A" "B" "C" "D" "E"


This would work for vectors of any length, for example:

week_days <- c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday")

# This works:
week_days[-length(week_days)]

[1] "Monday"  "Tuesday"

# Whereas our previous solution gives the wrong answer (it removes nothing):
week_days[-6]

[1] "Monday"    "Tuesday"   "Wednesday"






Define a list containing a character vector, a logical value, and another list:


mylist <- list(
  a = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday"),
  b = TRUE,
  c = list(rnorm(5), 21.3, "firstname")
)


Use subsetting to select:


The first element
The element named b
Tuesday
21.3







NoteSolution






# i.  The first element;

mylist[[1]]

[1] "Monday"    "Tuesday"   "Wednesday"

# ii. The element named `b`;

mylist$b

[1] TRUE

mylist[["b"]]

[1] TRUE

mylist["b"]

$b
[1] TRUE

mylist[names(mylist) == "b"]

$b
[1] TRUE

# iii. `Tuesday`

mylist[["a"]][2]

[1] "Tuesday"

mylist[[1]][2]

[1] "Tuesday"

# iv. `21.3`

mylist$c[[2]]

[1] 21.3

mylist[[3]][[2]]

[1] 21.3

title: Practical 2: Data manipulation
text:
This practical uses synthetic Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) data on hip fractures to practise the core dplyr verbs. It has two parts:
We’ll use the same data again in Session 3, when we combine it with other tables.
All data in this practical is simulated for teaching purposes.

title: Practical 2: Data manipulation
text:
Datasets




hes_admissions
One row per hospital spell. A spell is one continuous hospital stay, from admission to discharge.

spell_id, patient_id
Admission and discharge dates
Admission method and source
Discharge destination
Hospital (provider_code) and specialty
Length of stay in days (los_days)




hes_patients
One row per patient.

patient_id
Sex
Date of birth
Area deprivation (IMD quintile, where 1 is the most deprived)
Ethnicity
GP practice and region

title: Practical 2: Data manipulation
text:
Import
Download hes_admissions.csv and hes_patients.csv and save them in the folder you’re working in. Then load the tidyverse and import both files with read_csv():

library(tidyverse)

admissions <- read_csv("hes_admissions.csv")
patients <- read_csv("hes_patients.csv")

Part 1: First steps with dplyr

TipHint

title: Practical 2: Data manipulation
text:
Part 2: Creating and recoding columns
This part is done at the start of Session 3. If you’re starting afresh, re-run the import code first.

Add a column, los_weeks, with the length of stay in weeks (use mutate()).

Round it to one decimal place.
Select spell_id, los_days and los_weeks to check your answer.








NoteSolution






admissions |>
  mutate(los_weeks = round(los_days / 7, 1)) |>
  select(spell_id, los_days, los_weeks)

# A tibble: 6,711 × 3
   spell_id los_days los_weeks
   <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 S0000001     11.8       1.7
 2 S0000002     12.7       1.8
 3 S0000003     11.9       1.7
 4 S0000004     14.7       2.1
 5 S0000005     11.6       1.7
 6 S0000006     11.3       1.6
 7 S0000007      9.9       1.4
 8 S0000008     10.7       1.5
 9 S0000009      6.9       1  
10 S0000010      7.6       1.1
# ℹ 6,701 more rows






Create a column, long_stay, with mutate() and if_else().

“Yes” if the spell was longer than 14 days; “No” otherwise.
Use count() to see how many spells are in each group.

count(data, column) counts the rows for each value of a column, like table(). We’ll see more of it in Session 3.







NoteSolution






admissions |>
  mutate(long_stay = if_else(los_days > 14, "Yes", "No")) |>
  count(long_stay)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  long_stay     n
  <chr>     <int>
1 No         5137
2 Yes        1574


There are 1,574 long stays, matching what we found in question 4.
You could also store a logical (TRUE/FALSE) column directly, without if_else():

admissions |>
  mutate(long_stay = los_days > 14) |>
  count(long_stay)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  long_stay     n
  <lgl>     <int>
1 FALSE      5137
2 TRUE       1574






Clean discharge_destination: “UNK” and “Unknown” both mean the destination was not recorded.

Use count() to look at its values.
Use na_if() inside mutate() to replace both with proper missing values (NA).
Count again, and store the result by overwriting admissions.








TipHint





na_if(x, y) replaces any values of x that are equal to y with NA. For example, na_if(c("a", "UNK", "b"), "UNK") gives "a" NA "b". You can use it twice, once for each value.









NoteSolution






admissions |>
  count(discharge_destination)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  discharge_destination     n
  <chr>                 <int>
1 Care Home               955
2 Died                     70
3 Home                   3477
4 Rehabilitation         2008
5 UNK                      67
6 Unknown                  67
7 <NA>                     67

admissions <- admissions |>
  mutate(
    discharge_destination = na_if(discharge_destination, "UNK"),
    discharge_destination = na_if(discharge_destination, "Unknown")
  )

admissions |>
  count(discharge_destination)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  discharge_destination     n
  <chr>                 <int>
1 Care Home               955
2 Died                     70
3 Home                   3477
4 Rehabilitation         2008
5 <NA>                    201


Before recoding there were 67 spells each with “UNK” and “Unknown”, and 67 already missing (NA). The original file has empty values for these 67 spells, and read_csv() reads empty values as NA automatically. After recoding, all 201 unknown destinations are NA.




Group length of stay into three bands with case_when():

“Up to 7 days”
“7 to 14 days” (more than 7, up to 14)
“Over 14 days”

Count the number of spells in each band.







TipHint





Conditions in case_when() are checked in order, and each row gets the value from the first condition that is TRUE.









NoteSolution






admissions |>
  mutate(
    los_band = case_when(
      los_days <= 7 ~ "Up to 7 days",
      los_days <= 14 ~ "7 to 14 days",
      los_days > 14 ~ "Over 14 days"
    )
  ) |>
  count(los_band)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  los_band         n
  <chr>        <int>
1 7 to 14 days  4817
2 Over 14 days  1574
3 Up to 7 days   320


There are 320 spells up to 7 days, 4,817 between 7 and 14 days, and 1,574 over 14 days. Because the conditions are checked in order, the second condition (los_days <= 14) only applies to stays longer than 7 days.
Note that count() lists the bands in alphabetical order, not in order of length of stay.




Recode admission_method (a HES code) into a new column, admission_route:

21, an emergency admission via A&E, becomes “A&E”
22, an emergency admission via a GP, becomes “GP”

Use count() to check that every code has been recoded.







NoteSolution






admissions |>
  mutate(
    admission_route = case_when(
      admission_method == 21 ~ "A&E",
      admission_method == 22 ~ "GP"
    )
  ) |>
  count(admission_method, admission_route)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  admission_method admission_route     n
             <dbl> <chr>           <int>
1               21 A&E              4838
2               22 GP               1873


Counting both the old and new columns together is a quick way to check a recode: 4,838 spells were via A&E and 1,873 via a GP, with no NA values left over. Because there are only two codes, if_else(admission_method == 21, "A&E", "GP") would also work, but case_when() leaves any unexpected codes as NA, where you’ll notice them.









NoteGoing further…





Write a single pipeline that starts with admissions and:

creates long_stay (question 10) and los_band (question 12);
keeps spells where the patient was discharged home;
counts the number of spells by los_band and long_stay.



Show the solution
admissions |>
  mutate(
    long_stay = if_else(los_days > 14, "Yes", "No"),
    los_band = case_when(
      los_days <= 7 ~ "Up to 7 days",
      los_days <= 14 ~ "7 to 14 days",
      los_days > 14 ~ "Over 14 days"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(discharge_destination == "Home") |>
  count(los_band, long_stay)


# A tibble: 3 × 3
  los_band     long_stay     n
  <chr>        <chr>     <int>
1 7 to 14 days No         2849
2 Over 14 days Yes         414
3 Up to 7 days No          214
